0.title: Training Up Children in the Fear of the Lord
0.essay:
“Behold, children are a heritage from the LORD, the fruit of the womb a reward” (Psalm 127:3). That is not sentiment. It is theology.

God’s gift

Children are not our possessions, our projects or our legacy. They are God’s gift, entrusted to parents for a season, to be raised in the knowledge of the One who made them and loves them more than any parent ever could.

The greatest discipleship task

Christian parenting is the most significant discipleship task most believers will ever undertake. A parent has more sustained, intimate influence over a child than any pastor, teacher or mentor. What happens in the ordinary rhythms of home — eating, sleeping, playing, arguing, forgiving, reading, praying — shapes a child’s understanding of God, of themselves, of love and justice, and of what it means to be human, more deeply than almost anything else.

Privilege and responsibility

That is an extraordinary privilege and a sobering responsibility. The parent who grasps it need not be paralysed by anxiety about getting everything right. Instead, it drives them to their knees, to the word and to the church, knowing that the task is too large for any one parent, and that the God who gave the children has promised to be present in the raising of them.

The chapters

Children as Gift and Stewardship; The Shema: discipleship in the home; Discipline and Grace: the gospel shape of correction; The Father Heart of God: parenting from the overflow; Prodigals and Difficult Seasons; and Releasing and Entrusting: the long view of parenting.

For reflection

What do you most want your children, or the children in your church, to know about God by the time they leave home?

1.title: Children as Gift and Stewardship
1.essay:
Before we can parent well, we need to understand what children are. They are not blank slates, extensions of our identity, or instruments of our ambitions. They are image-bearers, entrusted to us for a season.

Persons, not projects

Every child, from conception, bears the image of God. Every child has dignity, personhood and moral significance, a soul and a relationship with God that no parent can replace or engineer. A child’s questions, fears, joys and worship are not rough sketches of adult experience. They are the real thing, offered by a real person to the real God.

This has huge practical consequences. A parent who treats a child as a project — something to shape, improve and display — tends to produce either a performer who has learned to work for approval, or a rebel who has decided that being themselves requires distance from the parent’s agenda. A parent who treats a child as a person, made in God’s image and loved by him, will parent with a different posture: not controlling but cultivating, not performing but serving, not owning but stewarding.

A heritage

The word heritage in Psalm 127:3 is the word used for the land of Canaan, the inheritance God gave his people as a covenant gift. Children belong in the same category. And reward does not mean children are earned; it describes the joy and good they bring. This reframes the modern question of whether to have children. The biblical framework is not mainly a lifestyle calculation, but receiving or declining a gift from God.

Unless the LORD builds

The same psalm begins, “Unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Psalm 127:1). Even the most diligent, thoughtful, theologically informed parenting depends finally on the sovereign grace of God who saves. Paul says of ministry, “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6). Parents plant and water. God gives the growth.

That does not make parenting passive. It makes it prayerful. And it releases parents from the crushing belief that their child’s spiritual outcome depends entirely on them.

Let the children come

When the disciples tried to turn children away, Jesus was indignant: “Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God” (Mark 10:14). Children are not on the edge of the kingdom. They are its picture. Not because they are innocent, for they are not, but because they are small, dependent and receive freely. That is the posture of every citizen of the kingdom. A parent who teaches a child to come to Jesus is teaching the most important thing that child will ever learn.

Lent to the LORD

Hannah prayed for a son with such intensity that Eli thought she was drunk. When God gave her Samuel, she brought him to the house of the LORD and said, “Therefore I have lent him to the LORD. As long as he lives, he is lent to the LORD” (1 Samuel 1:28).

That is a theology of parenthood in a sentence. She received him as a gift and returned him to the Giver. It was not detachment. “His mother used to make for him a little robe and take it to him each year” (1 Samuel 2:19). But she held him with an open hand. A parent who holds a child with a clenched fist will either crush the child or be crushed by the child’s choices. A parent who keeps offering the child back to God is freed from the anxiety of control.

Israel’s law made the same point. “Consecrate to me all the firstborn” (Exodus 13:2), God said: children are finally his, not their parents’.

Not alone

Israel’s children were raised within the covenant community, not merely within a household. Moses summoned the children to hear the law read (Deuteronomy 31:12), and the whole book of Deuteronomy is framed around passing faith on: “Make them known to your children and your children’s children” (Deuteronomy 4:9). That is a corrective to modern Western parenting, in which parents often carry the whole weight of a child’s formation alone. The church is meant to share it.

Telling the next generation

Psalm 78 is explicit about this design: “We will not hide them from their children, but tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the LORD, and his might, and the wonders that he has done” (Psalm 78:4). A parent who tells their children what God has done — in Scripture, in history and in their own life — is taking part in the great work of keeping the memory of God’s faithfulness alive on earth. A child who grows up hearing stories of God’s faithfulness has a very different foundation from one who hears only stories of human achievement.

A promise of wisdom

“Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it” (Proverbs 22:6). This is a proverb, a statement of wisdom about how life generally works: faithful formation bears lasting fruit. It is not an iron guarantee. It does not mean a faithfully raised child will never wander, or that a prodigal is proof of failed parenting. God himself is the perfect Father, and his children still wander. Our faithfulness is our responsibility. The child’s response is their own, and finally God’s to secure.

For reflection

Do you tend to treat your children, or the children around you, more as projects or as persons? What would holding them with an open hand look like this week?

2.title: The Shema: Comprehensive Discipleship in the Home
2.essay:
The most important passage in the Bible for Christian parents is not in the New Testament. It is Deuteronomy 6, the Shema, the creed every Israelite child grew up hearing.

The curriculum

“Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might” (Deuteronomy 6:4–5). That is the curriculum: the great commandment, to love God with everything.

The goal is not behavioural compliance but a devoted heart. A parent whose main goal is obedient behaviour tends to produce either a child who has learned to conform outwardly, or a rebel who has sensed that the real goal is control rather than love. A parent whose goal is love for God will parent differently: seeking to make God attractive, to show his goodness and to let the child taste his love, so that the child’s heart is drawn to him rather than driven.

On your heart first

Then the instruction: “And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children” (Deuteronomy 6:6–7). Notice the order. It begins with the parent’s own heart, not with a technique for teaching children. You cannot pass on what you do not possess.

A parent who is captivated by God — who prays, reads Scripture and lives with the love of God as their deepest motive — will find that their children catch what they carry, even before any formal teaching begins. Faith in the home is caught as well as taught.

The classroom is all of life

Moses goes on: you “shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise” (Deuteronomy 6:7). Sitting, walking, lying down, rising: the whole arc of a day. The instruction is not to add a religious programme to the schedule, but to make the whole schedule an occasion for faith.

The mealtime conversation, the bedtime prayer, the car journey, the morning rush: all are opportunities for faith to be spoken, shown and woven in. This is discipleship by immersion, and it is more powerful than any curriculum, because it shapes a child’s imagination and instincts as well as their mind.

From infancy

Paul reminds Timothy that “from childhood you have been acquainted with the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 3:15). The word means from infancy. This faith came through his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (2 Timothy 1:5). Three generations: the grandmother, the mother, and the result, one of Paul’s most trusted co-workers.

A parent who reads Scripture to children before they can understand every word is doing something profound. They are building the world of language and imagination within which the child will one day make sense of the gospel.

Train up a child

The Hebrew word behind “train” in Proverbs 22:6 is related to the dedication of a building: a founding act of orientation. “The way he should go” may also carry the sense of the way suited to that particular child. Early formation has lasting effects. Seeds planted in childhood may lie dormant for decades before they sprout. Some of the most moving testimonies to faithful parenting come from prodigals who, years later, returned to what they were taught.

Do not provoke

Paul gives two commands that belong together: “Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4). Do not exasperate them by unreasonable demands, inconsistency, favouritism, harshness, or crushing their personhood. And do bring them up, with both training and wise counsel.

A parent who disciplines without relationship provokes. A parent who nurtures without discipline fails to instruct. The gospel parent does both, building the trust within which correction is received rather than resented.

The home first

In Israel, the family was the first place of religious education. God chose Abraham “that he may command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the LORD” (Genesis 18:19). That does not diminish the role of the church. But it does make the home the primary place where faith is passed on, practised and lived. The church strengthens what the home does; the home cannot be outsourced to the church.

Family worship

The Puritans developed the practice of family worship — a daily gathering of the household for Scripture, prayer and song — as the most direct application of the Shema. Richard Baxter urged ministers to visit and catechise every family, convinced that the church is renewed as households are renewed. A family that prays together, even imperfectly, briefly, and through seasons of resistance, is building patterns of devotion that can last a lifetime.

For reflection

Where in your ordinary day — sitting, walking, lying down, rising — could you speak naturally of God with your children? What is on your own heart that they might catch?

3.title: Discipline and Grace: The Gospel Shape of Correction
3.essay:
Few areas of parenting cause more confusion and anxiety than discipline. Scripture’s teaching is clear but not simple. It calls for both firm correction and deep grace.

Two failures

A parent who applies discipline without grace will produce moralism and resentment. A parent who offers grace without discipline will raise a child who has never met the serious love of God that Hebrews describes. The Bible holds both together.

Love disciplines

Hebrews 12 is the key passage. “For the Lord disciplines the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6), as a father disciplines a son in whom he delights. Discipline is not punishment handed out by an angry authority. It is the loving formation offered by a Father committed to his child’s good, even when that good requires pain.

Proverbs puts it sharply: “Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is diligent to discipline him” (Proverbs 13:24). A parent who cannot bear to correct, who cares more about a child’s momentary happiness than their formation, is in effect failing to love them. The child who is never corrected has missed one of the basic forms of a parent’s love.

Formation, not payment

God “disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness” (Hebrews 12:10). Its purpose is not to pay off a debt but to form holiness. Punishment looks back to what was done. Discipline looks forward to who the person is becoming. A parent who disciplines for formation will do it with clarity about the behaviour, compassion for the child’s heart, consistency, and confidence in the goal.

And it keeps two horizons in view: “For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it” (Hebrews 12:11). The tears and resistance of the moment are the price of future fruit. Grasping that frees a parent from guilt over short-term pain that serves long-term good.

The rod

Proverbs speaks of the rod of discipline several times (Proverbs 13:24; 22:15; 23:13–14; 29:15): “Folly is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of discipline drives it far from him” (Proverbs 22:15). These texts have caused real debate. Most Reformed scholars understand them to commend appropriate physical correction as one tool among many, used with restraint, connected to relationship, and suited to the child’s age. That is the most likely reading.

But harshness is forbidden. A parent who uses physical discipline carelessly, angrily or excessively has left the biblical pattern and moved into harm. A parent who abandons all correction as harmful has also left it, for a permissiveness Proverbs calls hatred of the child.

Do not discourage

Paul’s warning in Colossians is even simpler than in Ephesians: “Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged” (Colossians 3:21). To be discouraged is to lose heart. A child who is constantly criticised, never affirmed, held to impossible standards, or corrected in anger eventually gives up, withdraws or rebels. Relationship is the channel through which all correction travels. Damage the relationship and the instruction stops getting through.

The heart behind the behaviour

Tedd Tripp, in Shepherding a Child’s Heart, observes that discipline which only addresses behaviour is like cutting a weed at ground level: the root remains. The parent’s aim is to understand what the child’s heart was doing — what did they want, fear or try to control? — and to address that as well. That takes conversation as well as correction, and a genuine interest in the child as a person rather than a problem to solve.

Eli’s failure

Eli the priest had wicked sons, and God judged him “because his sons were blaspheming God, and he did not restrain them” (1 Samuel 3:13). God charged him with choosing to “honor your sons above me” (1 Samuel 2:29). Eli’s failure was not personal wickedness. It was a refusal to exercise loving authority. A parent who will not discipline because they want to be liked, or cannot bear their child’s displeasure, repeats his error.

Grace in correction

Every act of discipline is a chance to preach the gospel. When a child is corrected, they experience something of what God’s law does: it shows that what they did was wrong, that wrong has consequences, and that relationship is at stake. When correction is followed by forgiveness, reassurance of love and restored relationship, they experience something of what the gospel does.

The father in the parable of the prodigal son shows the shape of it. He let the son face the consequences of his choices. He watched with longing. And “while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him” (Luke 15:20). A family that corrects and restores, disciplines and forgives, is living out the gospel at the kitchen table.

For reflection

Are you more prone to correction without grace, or grace without correction? What would it look like to follow discipline with clear forgiveness and restored relationship?

4.title: The Father Heart of God: Parenting from the Overflow
4.essay:
The most important thing a Christian parent can do for their child is to know God as Father. Not just the doctrine, but the living God who runs to prodigals.

Parenting from what we have received

This is the God who numbers the hairs of his children’s heads, who neither slumbers nor sleeps as he watches over them, who works all things together for their good, who disciplines them for their holiness, and who has prepared an eternal home for them. A parent who knows this God parents from the overflow of that knowledge.

A parent who relates to God mainly through duty, guilt or performance anxiety will almost inevitably parent the same way: demanding performance, giving approval conditionally, keeping the relationship going through the child’s compliance. That is not mainly a personality problem. It is a theological one. And the cure is not better technique, but a deeper experience of the Father’s love.

Every family named

Paul writes, “For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named” (Ephesians 3:14–15). Human fatherhood and motherhood are not accidental biological facts. They reflect something of God himself. That humbles us, because we are dim reflections of the original. And it encourages us, because the original is available to us, and his Spirit will supply what our nature lacks.

Paul goes on to pray that his readers would “know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge” (Ephesians 3:19). Only someone flooded with that love has enough to give it away lavishly. The parent who has been loved well by God can love a child generously, not because they are naturally patient, but because they are drawing from a source that does not run dry.

Abba, Father

“You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons” (Romans 8:15), by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!” The Spirit enables a Christian to know God as Father in their bones, not merely in their theology. A parent who brings their fears, failures and joys to the Father with the freedom of an adopted child does not parent alone. They parent from within the Father’s embrace.

J. I. Packer, in Knowing God, called this the highest privilege of the Christian life: “a Christian is one who has God as Father.” A parent who knows, not merely believes, that God is their Father has a resource no technique or curriculum can supply.

More than a mother

God uses the image of a nursing mother to describe his love: “Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you” (Isaiah 49:15). He takes the most instinctive, self-giving love in human experience, and then exceeds it. A parent’s fierce love for a child reflects God’s own love. And a child who knows that God loves them even more than their parents do has found a security no human love can provide.

The fruit the child needs

Read the fruit of the Spirit as a description of the parent every child needs: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Where does this come from? Not from natural virtue, parenting courses, or even enough sleep, though that helps. It comes from the Spirit.

So the parent who is patient with a child is not drawing on a private reservoir of patience. They are showing fruit the Spirit is producing. “Lord, give me patience with my child” is a prayer the Spirit delights to answer. The most important thing a parent can do for their children is to grow in the Spirit themselves.

Pointing beyond ourselves

Jesus taught us to pray “Our Father.” Every good human father is a dim reflection of that perfect Father, and every failure of human parenting is an opportunity to point children beyond us to him. A parent who admits their failures to their children and points them to the Father who never fails is doing something profoundly theological.

A calling, not an identity

A parent who has made parenting their primary identity, whose sense of worth rises and falls with their children’s performance, has made parenting an idol. The results are painful: anxious, smothering involvement; collapse when a child makes poor choices; inability to release them into adulthood. A parent whose identity is in Christ can parent with both intensity and freedom: intense because they love deeply, free because their worth does not depend on the outcome.

The father who ran

The father in Luke 15 is the Bible’s fullest portrait of the Father’s heart, and so of the heart Christian parents are called to show. He lets the son go; he does not chain him to duty. He watches; he does not forget or harden. He runs; he does not stand on his dignity or wait for a complete apology. He restores lavishly, with robe, ring and feast; he imposes no probation. It is extravagant, undignified love. And a parent who prays to love like this is praying a prayer the Father, who runs to his own prodigals, delights to answer.

For reflection

Do you relate to God more through duty and performance, or as a loved child? How might that be shaping the way you parent? Which fruit of the Spirit do you most need to pray for today?

5.title: Prodigals and Difficult Seasons
5.essay:
Every generation of Christian parents has had prodigals: children raised in the faith, prayed for and taught the Scriptures, who have nonetheless walked away.

A particular grief

Some children struggle with addiction, broken relationships, confusion about identity, or a hardness towards God that breaks their parents’ hearts. This is not a new problem. It is the oldest one: human freedom and the mystery of God’s sovereignty.

A parent of a prodigal carries a grief unlike almost any other: watching someone you love choose a path you know leads to harm, being unable to stop it, praying without visible answer, loving a person who may not want your love. That grief is real and legitimate. The Bible does not pretend that faithful parenting always produces faithful children, and it does not ask the parent of a prodigal to pretend either.

What such parents need

They need three things. First, a theological framework that frees them from the crushing belief that the outcome is all their fault. Second, practical wisdom about keeping a relationship with a child whose choices they cannot affirm. Third, the church, to sustain them in prayer and friendship through the long, often invisible work of waiting. None of these comes from a technique. They require the gospel, wisdom and the body of Christ.

Sovereignty and freedom

Parents of prodigals inevitably wrestle with God’s sovereignty. Did God ordain this? Could he have prevented it? Reformed theology does not flinch: God is sovereign over all things, including a prodigal’s choices. But his sovereignty does not make those choices unchosen. The child is genuinely choosing. Both are true, and the parent must hold that tension without full resolution in this life.

The comfort is this: the God who is sovereign over all things loves the prodigal more than the parent does, and he has not given up.

He came to himself

In Jesus’ parable, the turning point came when the younger son was feeding pigs: “But when he came to himself” (Luke 15:17), he remembered his father’s house. That moment of clarity was not produced by lectures or manipulation. It came through his circumstances and, we would say, the work of the Spirit. Parents cannot engineer that moment. They can pray for it, stay present for it, and be ready with open arms when it comes.

The ministry of watching

“While he was still a long way off, his father saw him” (Luke 15:20). The father was watching. He was not passive. He was attentive, ready. The parent of a prodigal is called to this ministry of watching and waiting: praying persistently, keeping the relationship open, communicating love without condoning choices, and believing that return is possible. It is the faith that keeps the light on and the door unlocked.

When should a parent speak, and when be silent? The father in Luke 15 did not lecture the departing son. He did not plead or bargain. He let the consequences do their work, and he was ready and joyful at the return. That is not indifference. It is respect for the child as a person, and trust that God can speak to the child’s heart without the parent’s constant intervention.

Many parents instead withdraw: emotionally, to protect themselves; relationally, to punish the child; or theologically, deciding the child is beyond grace. The father in the parable did none of these. A parent who stays present, loving without approving and keeping contact without endorsing choices, keeps the path home open.

New every morning

Lamentations was written in the rubble of Jerusalem, after everything was destroyed. The parent of a prodigal knows something of that devastation. And these words are a lifeline: “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:22–23). Not used up by last night’s grief, or by years of unanswered prayer. A parent who cannot see what God is doing can still affirm who God is.

Nothing can separate

Paul writes that nothing “in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:39). The love that pursues God’s children is stronger than the choices that lead them away. The parent is not the last line of defence between the prodigal and destruction. God is, and his love, which went to the cross, is more patient and resourceful than any human love.

Cast your anxieties

The anxiety of a prodigal season is heavy. Peter gives both an instruction and a permission: “casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). The word means to throw, a deliberate transfer. The fear for the child’s safety, the grief, the confusion about what to say — all of it. God can bear what is crushing you. And the God who cares for the anxious parent cares equally for the wandering child.

The son of these tears

Monica prayed for her wayward son Augustine for many years, through his immorality, his intellectual wandering and his involvement with a false religion. When he deceived her and sailed to Italy without her, she followed. She prayed, wept and persisted. A bishop she pleaded with told her, “It is not possible that the son of these tears should perish,” as Augustine recalls in his Confessions. His return came, and it was one of the most significant conversions in church history. Monica’s prayers were part of it.

For reflection

If you are waiting for a prodigal, what anxiety do you need to cast on God today? How can you keep the door open without approving what you cannot affirm? Who in your church could you support who is walking this road?

6.title: Releasing and Entrusting: The Long View of Parenting
6.essay:
The goal of Christian parenting is not a child who needs their parent for ever. It is a person so rooted in God that they can walk with him faithfully through their whole independent life.

Working yourself out of a job

A parent who has done this well has worked themselves out of the primary discipling role. The measure of success is not that the child never leaves, but that when they leave, they are ready: formed by faith, established in character, connected to the church.

The same verse that grounds marriage grounds this release: “a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife” (Genesis 2:24). The leaving is the child’s act, but it needs the parent’s blessing. A parent who has been gradually handing over responsibility as maturity grows will not be blindsided when the leaving comes. They will celebrate it, as the sign of work well done.

The hardest release

Releasing is one of the most emotionally demanding things parents face. A parent who cannot release a child is holding on to something that was always God’s, imposing a dependence that was always meant to be temporary, and preventing growth that can only happen in independence.

Abraham’s test was whether he would withhold his most treasured gift from God. The angel said, “for now I know that you fear God, seeing you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me” (Genesis 22:12). And God provided the ram. The God who calls us to release our children has not abandoned them. He has received them.

That offering takes many forms: the infant in dedication, the teenager in prayer when the parent cannot control the outcome, the adult child who makes choices the parent would not have made. In every case, not withholding — releasing control and trusting God — is the act of parental faith.

He will complete it

Paul’s confidence in the Philippians is a parent’s confidence too: “And I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). The parent does not complete the work. They take part in a work God began before the child was born and will finish on the day of Christ. The outcome is not in your hands. Your calling is faithfulness; his is completion.

A long obedience

Eugene Peterson’s phrase, “a long obedience in the same direction,” fits parenting well. No programme produces results in a month. Forming a human being is the work of decades: consistent, faithful, unglamorous, daily. A parent who commits to faithful presence, daily prayer, steady love, honest correction and joyful celebration will one day look back and see what they could not see while doing it: the hand of God in the whole story.

Seeds you may not see

Lois and Eunice’s faithfulness shaped Timothy into one of the great gospel workers of the apostolic age. By the time Paul wrote 2 Timothy, they may well have died. Parents plant some seeds they will see sprout in their lifetime, and others they will not. The harvest belongs to God; the planting is our calling.

Psalm 78 has this long view: “that the next generation might know them, the children yet unborn, and arise and tell them to their children, so that they should set their hope in God” (Psalm 78:6–7). A parent who teaches a child is already thinking of grandchildren not yet born. Every bedtime prayer and every honest moment of faith is a thread in a tapestry that stretches across generations.

The long view

Then comes the next stage: watching an adult child navigate their own faith, marriage and parenting. Praying across the distance. Offering wisdom when asked, holding back when not. Becoming the grandparent who prays for the next generation. This is the intergenerational work of the kingdom, a chain of testimony and trust stretching across the decades until Christ returns.

Blessing

Scripture is full of parents blessing their children: Isaac blessing his sons, Jacob blessing his twelve, Moses blessing the tribes. Many Christian families have lost this practice. To bless a child is to speak specifically and intentionally about who they are, what gifts you see in them, what hope you have for their future, and what God’s hand has been doing in their life. It says: I see you, I love you, I release you, and I trust the God who made you to finish what he has begun.

The ancient priestly blessing is a fitting benediction over a child being released:

“The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace” (Numbers 6:24–26).

It is the parent’s deepest prayer. It is also the promise of the God who receives the child they offer.

For reflection

What would it mean for you to hold your children with an open hand at their present stage? Consider writing or speaking a blessing over each of your children, or over a young person in your church.
